title: Math is Mine
contentObjective: I can look back at my answers from Lesson 1-1, describe how my math biography has changed this year, and recognize ways we are all doers of math.
languageObjective: I can compare my beginning-of-year and end-of-year math stories using the words then, now, changed, and grown.

turnAndTalk.question: In September you estimated 20 cars × 4 riders = about 80 Ferris wheel riders per turn. Now, at 6 turns an hour, how many riders per hour — and what tool did you use that you didn't have in September?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 80 riders per turn × 6 turns an hour = 480 riders an hour, using a rate — a tool this year's math added.

stems.en: The Ferris wheel carries about ___ riders an hour because ___.
stems.es: La rueda de la fortuna lleva alrededor de ___ pasajeros por hora porque ___.

stems.en: I used a ___ this year that I did not have in September.
stems.es: Este año usé una ___ que no tenía en septiembre.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer multiplies 80 × 6 = 480 correctly and names 'rate' as the new tool. A weak answer gives 480 with no explanation of what changed since September.
turnAndTalk.extend: The wheel now runs 480 riders an hour. If it operates for 5 hours, how many total riders is that — and how is this calculation an even bigger extension of your September math?
extendStems: In 5 hours, the wheel carries ___ riders because ___.
This extends my September math because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted skills into 'I could already do this in September' and 'I learned or grew into this during Grade 6,' what made 'dividing a fraction by a fraction' belong in the growth column?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Dividing fractions, using ratios and unit rates, plotting all four quadrants, and solving one-variable equations are new tools Grade 6 added — not skills from September.

stems.en: Dividing fractions belongs in the growth column because ___.
stems.es: Dividir fracciones pertenece a la columna de crecimiento porque ___.

stems.en: Estimating the Ferris wheel stayed in September because ___.
stems.es: Estimar la rueda de la fortuna se quedó en septiembre porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students distinguishing skills that existed before the year started from skills built during Grade 6 — not just listing skills without sorting them.
turnAndTalk.extend: Pick one skill from the growth column and explain how it changes the way you would solve a problem from September, like the Ferris wheel estimate.
extendStems: Using ___, I could now solve the Ferris wheel problem by ___.
This is different from September because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: In September you decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5. This year you learned 78.5 = 157 ÷ 2 and 50% of 157 = 78.5. How does comparing these show your math story changing?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The same number, 78.5, can now be reached through division and percents — tools that didn't exist in your September toolbox.

stems.en: My math story changed because I can now write 78.5 using ___, not just ___.
stems.es: Mi historia matemática cambió porque ahora puedo escribir 78.5 usando ___, no solo ___.

stems.en: One new way to write 78.5 is ___.
stems.es: Una nueva forma de escribir 78.5 es ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer names a specific new method (division or percent) and connects it back to 78.5 correctly, not just claiming 'I know more now.'
turnAndTalk.extend: Ask a classmate for one new way THEY found to write 78.5. Compare it to yours — what's the same, and what's different about the tools you each used?
extendStems: This is the same as mine because ___, and different because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when you compared your September answers to your answers now, what strategy helped you notice real growth instead of just repeating your old answer?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Real growth shows up when you can explain WHY a method works, not just follow its steps the same way you did in September.

stems.en: I noticed growth by comparing ___ to ___.
I knew it was real growth because ___.
stems.es: Supe que era crecimiento real porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific comparison strategy tied to explaining reasoning, not just "I got better."
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who wrote the exact same answer they wrote in Lesson 1-1, with nothing new added? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.

launch.narrative: Throughout this school year, you have seen math used in many different activities and used it to solve different kinds of problems. Today you look back at the answers you wrote to the questions in Lesson 1-1 — and see how far your math story has come.

conceptIntro.heading: Your math story, one year later
conceptIntro.intro: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated riders on a Ferris wheel, decomposed 78.5, and wrote your math story. The question now is not 'what is math?' but 'how have I changed as a doer of math?'
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Mathematical Reflection & Portfolio Culmination. 1. Synthesize grade-level mastery across Number Systems, Ratios, Expressions, Geometry, and Statistics. 2. Justify problem-solving strategies using multiple representations (equations, graphs, models). 3. Reflect on mathematical growth and communicate solutions with precision and confidence

iDo.title: Watch me reread my September work
lines: In September I estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4 = 80 riders — 'about 80.'
Now I can go further with this year's math: at 6 turns an hour, that wheel moves about 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour.
Same wheel, same me — but my toolbox grew. That difference IS my math story.
linesEs: En septiembre estimé la rueda de la fortuna: 20 cabinas con unas 4 personas cada una son 20 × 4 = 80 personas — «unas 80».
Ahora puedo ir más lejos con las matemáticas de este año: a 6 vueltas por hora, esa rueda mueve unas 80 × 6 = 480 personas por hora.
La misma rueda, el mismo yo — pero mi caja de herramientas creció. Esa diferencia es mi historia matemática.
iDo.titleEs: Mírame releer mi trabajo de septiembre

conceptIntro.introEs: En la lección 1-1 estimaste cuántas personas subían a una rueda de la fortuna, descompusiste 78.5 y escribiste tu historia matemática. Ahora la pregunta no es «¿qué son las matemáticas?» sino «¿cómo he cambiado yo al hacer matemáticas?»
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Reflexión matemática y cierre del portafolio. 1. Integra el dominio del grado en sistemas numéricos, razones, expresiones, geometría y estadística. 2. Justifica tus estrategias de resolución usando varias representaciones (ecuaciones, gráficas, modelos). 3. Reflexiona sobre tu crecimiento matemático y comunica tus soluciones con precisión y confianza

connect.scenario: You and your classmates each wrote about your math stories at the beginning of the school year. Everyone has their own math story, and as you encounter new challenges and experiences, your story might change.
connect.promptQuestion: How does your classmate's end-of-school-year math story compare to your story?
connect.prompt: Describe how your math story has ___ this year, ask a ___ about their story, and then ___ the two to see how they are alike and different.

check.stem: In September you estimated the Ferris wheel as 20 cars × 4 riders = about 80. Which of these uses a tool you did NOT have in September to extend that same estimate?
choices: Multiplying the 80 riders per turn by 6 turns per hour to find a rate of 480 riders per hour
Adding the 20 cars and 4 riders together to get 24
Guessing a completely different, unrelated number
Deciding not to estimate the Ferris wheel at all
check.explanation: 80 × 6 = 480 uses a rate, a tool this year's math added — the September estimate of 20 × 4 could not do this. Adding 20 + 4 or guessing does not use any new math tool at all.

check.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a real comparison of math stories with a classmate from just repeating what you already believe?
choices: Naming something the classmate actually said, plus one genuine similarity AND one genuine difference between the two stories
Writing 'we both got better at math' and stopping there
Copying your own September answer word for word
Skipping the classmate entirely and writing only about yourself
check.explanation: The lesson's check requires reporting something the classmate actually said and naming a genuine similarity and a genuine difference — a vague claim like 'we both got better' does not show that any real conversation happened.

check.stem: A student writes, 'My classmate's story changed the same way mine did — we both feel more confident now.' What is missing from this comparison?
choices: A genuine DIFFERENCE between the two stories, not just a shared similarity
The classmate's full name and grade
The exact date Lesson 1-1 was taught
A drawing of the Ferris wheel
check.explanation: A complete comparison names both a similarity and a difference; this answer only states a similarity, so it does not meet the lesson's check for a complete answer.

connect.modelAnswer: My classmate said that in September he only felt safe in math when he could copy an example, and now he tries problems first and checks the example after. We both got more comfortable being wrong on a first try. But our stories differ: his confidence grew most in equations, while mine grew most in ratios, because I started using unit rates when I shop with my mom.

approaching.stem: In Lesson 1-1 you estimated the Ferris wheel: 20 cars each holding about 4 people. About how many riders was that?
choices: About 80
About 24
About 5
About 400
approaching.explanation: 20 × 4 = 80 — the same estimate you made in September, and it still holds up.
choiceFeedback: That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: This is the very first estimate of the year — 20 groups of 4.
Multiply the cars by the riders per car.
approaching.stemEs: En la Lección 1-1 estimaste la rueda de la fortuna: 20 cabinas con unas 4 personas cada una. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros eran?
approaching.explanationEs: 20 × 4 = 80 — la misma estimación que hiciste en septiembre, y sigue siendo válida.
hintsEs: Esta es la primerísima estimación del año — 20 grupos de 4.
Multiplica las cabinas por los pasajeros de cada una.

approaching.stem: How has your attitude about math changed over the year?
approaching.modelAnswer: In September I thought being good at math meant being fast. Now I think it means sticking with a problem — some of my best work this year came on the second or third try.
sentenceStems: In September I thought math was ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cómo ha cambiado tu actitud hacia las matemáticas durante el año?

approaching.stem: In September you decomposed 78.5 as 70 + 8.5. Which of these ALSO equals 78.5, using division?
approaching.explanation: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, so it is another way to write the same number from Lesson 1-1.
choiceFeedback: 156 ÷ 2 = 78, which drops the 0.5.
78.5 ÷ 2 = 39.25 — that halves the number instead of rebuilding it.
hints: Which quotient lands exactly on 78.5?
Try doubling 78.5 first.
Double 78.5 first. The number you land on is the one being divided by 2.
approaching.stemEs: En septiembre descompusiste 78.5 como 70 + 8.5. ¿Cuál de estas TAMBIÉN es igual a 78.5, usando división?
approaching.explanationEs: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, así que es otra manera de escribir el mismo número de la Lección 1-1.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál cociente cae exactamente en 78.5?
Prueba duplicar primero 78.5.
Duplica primero 78.5. El número al que llegas es el que se está dividiendo entre 2.

approaching.stem: How have you used math at home or with your family in new or different ways this year?
approaching.modelAnswer: This year I started comparing prices with unit rates at the grocery store — I figured out which size of cereal actually costs less per ounce, which I never thought to do before Grade 6.
sentenceStems: This year at home I used math to ___ .
That was new for me because ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cómo has usado las matemáticas en casa o con tu familia de maneras nuevas o distintas este año?

approaching.stem: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea about math stories?
choices: Our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Your math story was finished when you wrote it in September
Only students with high grades have a math story
A math story never changes once it is written
approaching.explanation: The summary says it directly: we are all doers of math, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow and advance.
choiceFeedback: September was the BEGINNING of this year's story — today's lesson exists because the story kept going.
Everyone has a math story; being a doer of math is not about grades.
The whole point of comparing September to June is that the story DID change.
hints: Why are you rereading Lesson 1-1 today?
Because something changed between then and now.
Stories grow and evolve — which option says that?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál enunciado coincide con la gran idea de esta lección sobre las historias matemáticas?
approaching.explanationEs: El resumen lo dice directamente: todos hacemos matemáticas, y nuestras historias matemáticas siguen creciendo y cambiando conforme crecemos y avanzamos.
hintsEs: ¿Por qué estás releyendo la Lección 1-1 hoy?
Porque algo cambió entre entonces y ahora.
Las historias crecen y cambian — ¿cuál opción dice eso?

approaching.stem: As a result of what we learned together this year, where do you see math used in your community?
approaching.modelAnswer: I see math at the rec center scoreboard, in the percent-off signs at the store, and in the bus schedule my neighbor reads every morning. After this year I also notice ratios — like the mix on the snowball stand's price list.
sentenceStems: In my community I see math at ___ .
This year taught me to also notice ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Como resultado de lo que aprendimos juntos este año, ¿dónde ves que se usan las matemáticas en tu comunidad?

approaching.instructions: Sort each idea from this year into the unit of mathematics it belongs to.
approaching.instructionsEs: Clasifica cada idea de este año en la unidad de matemáticas a la que pertenece.
approaching.label: Sort this year's ideas into their areas of mathematics.
approaching.labelEs: Clasifica las ideas de este año en sus áreas de matemáticas.

categories.label: Statistics
items: The median of a data set
A dot plot of class data
itemsEs: La mediana de un conjunto de datos
Un diagrama de puntos con datos de la clase

hints: Percents compare to 100; statistics describes data; algebra relates variables.
Ask what each idea is FOR: estimating a part, summarizing data, or connecting two quantities.
hintsEs: Los porcentajes comparan con 100; la estadística describe datos; el álgebra relaciona variables.
Pregunta para qué sirve cada idea: estimar una parte, resumir datos o conectar dos cantidades.
approaching.explanation: This is the year in one sort: percents (50% of 157, benchmarks) compare quantities to 100; statistics (median, dot plots) summarizes collected data; algebra (y = kx, independent variables) connects quantities that change together. In September these were six unknown phrases — now they file themselves.
approaching.explanationEs: Este es el año en una sola clasificación: los porcentajes (50% de 157, referencias) comparan cantidades con 100; la estadística (mediana, diagramas de puntos) resume datos recolectados; el álgebra (y = kx, variables independientes) conecta cantidades que cambian juntas. En septiembre eran seis frases desconocidas; ahora se clasifican solas.

onLevel.stem: Now stretch the September estimate with this year's math: about 80 riders per turn, 6 turns each hour. About how many riders per hour?
choices: About 480
About 86
About 13
About 800
onLevel.explanation: 80 riders on each of 6 turns is 80 × 6 = 480 riders per hour — a rate, one of this year's tools.
choiceFeedback: That adds 80 + 6 instead of multiplying.
That divides 80 by 6 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 6.
hints: Each turn carries a full load of about 80.
There are 6 turns in an hour.
onLevel.stemEs: Ahora amplía la estimación de septiembre con las matemáticas de este año: unos 80 pasajeros por vuelta, 6 vueltas por hora. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros por hora?
onLevel.explanationEs: 80 pasajeros en cada una de 6 vueltas es 80 × 6 = 480 pasajeros por hora — una tasa, una de las herramientas de este año.
hintsEs: Cada vuelta lleva una carga completa de unos 80.
Hay 6 vueltas en una hora.

onLevel.stem: Percents were new this year. What is 50% of 157?
onLevel.explanation: 50% means half, and 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — the very number you decomposed back in Lesson 1-1.
choiceFeedback: 77.5 is half of 155, not 157.
107 subtracts 50 from 157 instead of taking 50 percent.
hints: 50% of a number is half of it.
Half of 157 means 157 ÷ 2.
Check your answer by doubling it — you should land back on 157.
onLevel.stemEs: Los porcentajes fueron nuevos este año. ¿Cuánto es el 50% de 157?
onLevel.explanationEs: 50% significa la mitad, y 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5 — el mismo número que descompusiste en la Lección 1-1.
hintsEs: El 50% de un número es su mitad.
La mitad de 157 significa 157 ÷ 2.
Revisa tu respuesta duplicándola — debes volver a 157.

onLevel.stem: What challenges did you face in math this year, and how did you respond to these challenges?
onLevel.modelAnswer: Dividing fractions was my biggest challenge — my first quiz did not go well. I responded by drawing models before using the rule, and by asking my partner to explain her way. By the next unit I could explain WHY dividing by one-half doubles a number.
sentenceStems: My biggest challenge this year was ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Qué retos enfrentaste en matemáticas este año, y cómo respondiste a esos retos?

onLevel.stem: Which of these is the strongest evidence that YOUR math reasoning grew this year?
choices: You can explain why a method works, not just follow its steps
You finish worksheets faster than in September
You memorized more answers than before
You stopped making any mistakes
onLevel.explanation: Constructing and explaining reasoning is the growth this lesson asks you to look for — it is what makes the math yours.
choiceFeedback: Speed can grow without understanding growing — it is not evidence of reasoning.
Memorized answers work only on problems you have already seen; reasoning works on new ones.
Nobody stopped making mistakes — growth shows in how you respond to them.
hints: Think about reasoning, not speed or memory.
Which option is about understanding WHY?
Explaining why a method works shows the math is yours.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es la evidencia más fuerte de que TU razonamiento matemático creció este año?
onLevel.explanationEs: Construir y explicar tu razonamiento es el crecimiento que esta lección te pide buscar — es lo que hace que las matemáticas sean tuyas.
hintsEs: Piensa en el razonamiento, no en la rapidez ni en la memoria.
¿Cuál opción se trata de entender POR QUÉ?
Explicar por qué funciona un método muestra que las matemáticas son tuyas.

onLevel.stem: Ask a classmate about their math story. How has your classmate's math story changed since the beginning of the year?
onLevel.modelAnswer: My classmate told me she used to erase everything the moment it looked wrong. Now she keeps her first attempt and writes the fix next to it, because seeing the mistake helped her on the ratio unit. Her story changed from hiding mistakes to using them.
sentenceStems: At the beginning of the year, my classmate ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Pregúntale a un compañero sobre su historia matemática. ¿Cómo ha cambiado su historia matemática desde el principio del año?

onLevel.stem: In what areas are you more confident about math now? What are your strengths in math?
onLevel.modelAnswer: I am most confident with ratios and unit rates now — I can set up a table and trust it. My strengths are estimating before I solve, which I already had in September, and explaining my steps out loud, which grew this year.
sentenceStems: I am more confident in ___ than I was in September.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿En qué áreas te sientes con más confianza en matemáticas ahora? ¿Cuáles son tus fortalezas en matemáticas?

onLevel.label: Answer each quick problem with this year's skills — the same numbers you met in Lesson 1-1.
onLevel.labelEs: Responde cada problema rápido con las destrezas de este año: los mismos números que viste en la Lección 1-1.

rows.problem: Riders per hour: 80 per turn × 6 turns

hints: 50% is a half; 10% moves the decimal one place left.
The Ferris wheel numbers are from your September estimate — solve them with June skills.
hintsEs: 50% es la mitad; 10% mueve el decimal un lugar a la izquierda.
Los números de la rueda de la fortuna son de tu estimación de septiembre: resuélvelos con destrezas de junio.
onLevel.explanation: Half of 157 is 78.5 — the very number Lesson 1-1 asked you to decompose in September. 10% of 480 moves the decimal to 48, and the Ferris wheel still carries 80 × 6 = 480 riders an hour. Same numbers, new power: that difference is the portfolio's evidence of growth.
onLevel.explanationEs: La mitad de 157 es 78.5, el mismísimo número que la Lección 1-1 te pidió descomponer en septiembre. El 10% de 480 mueve el decimal a 48, y la rueda de la fortuna sigue llevando 80 × 6 = 480 pasajeros por hora. Los mismos números con un poder nuevo: esa diferencia es la evidencia de crecimiento del portafolio.

extending.stem: Which set shows THREE correct ways to write 78.5 using skills from this year?
extending.explanation: All three rebuild 78.5 exactly: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, 50% of 157 = 78.5, and 78½ = 78.5.
choiceFeedback: 78¼ = 78.25, so that set contains an error.
156 ÷ 2 = 78, so that set contains an error.
25% of 157 = 39.25, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set against 78.5.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all three land exactly on 78.5.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál conjunto muestra TRES maneras correctas de escribir 78.5 usando destrezas de este año?
extending.explanationEs: Las tres reconstruyen 78.5 exactamente: 157 ÷ 2 = 78.5, 50% de 157 = 78.5, y 78½ = 78.5.
hintsEs: Revisa cada miembro de cada conjunto contra 78.5.
Un solo miembro incorrecto arruina todo el conjunto.
Halla el conjunto donde las tres caen exactamente en 78.5.

extending.stem: How have your math thinking HABITS changed from the beginning of the year to now? (Not what you know — how you think.)
extending.modelAnswer: In September my habit was to answer fast and move on. Now my habits are to estimate first so I can judge my answer, to try a second strategy when the first stalls, and to ask 'does this make sense?' before calling anything done. The facts I learned may fade, but I think these habits will stay.
sentenceStems: My old habit was ___ ; my new habit is ___ .
The habit I most want to keep is ___ because ___ .
extending.stemEs: ¿Cómo han cambiado tus HÁBITOS de pensamiento matemático desde el principio del año hasta ahora? (No lo que sabes — cómo piensas.)

extending.stem: Write a short letter to your September self. Tell them one thing about their math story that will change, and one piece of advice for the year ahead.
extending.modelAnswer: Dear September me: right now you think 'about 80 riders' is the best you can do with that Ferris wheel — by June you will turn it into 480 riders per hour without blinking. My advice: when the fraction unit gets hard in the winter, do not erase your wrong answers. You are going to learn more from them than from the right ones.
sentenceStems: Dear September me: one thing that will change is ___ .
extending.stemEs: Escribe una carta corta a la persona que eras en septiembre. Dile una cosa de su historia matemática que va a cambiar y un consejo para el año que viene.

extending.stem: We are always growing and changing. Think about who you were five years ago and who you are now. In what ways have you changed? In what ways have you grown?
extending.modelAnswer: Five years ago I was learning to multiply and I needed someone to tell me if I was right. I have changed in what I can do — fractions, ratios, negative numbers, equations — but I have grown more in how I work: I check my own answers, I can explain my thinking to someone else, and I expect hard problems to take more than one try.
sentenceStems: Five years ago I ___ ; now I ___ .
extending.stemEs: Siempre estamos creciendo y cambiando. Piensa en quién eras hace cinco años y quién eres ahora. ¿En qué maneras has cambiado? ¿En qué maneras has crecido?

extending.label: Match each September estimate to the refined result your math produces now.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada estimación de septiembre con el resultado refinado que tus matemáticas producen ahora.
hints: Each left card is a September question; each right card is where this year's skills take it.
Chain the estimates: riders per turn → riders per hour → riders per evening.
hintsEs: Cada tarjeta izquierda es una pregunta de septiembre; cada derecha es adonde la llevan las destrezas de este año.
Encadena las estimaciones: pasajeros por vuelta → por hora → por noche.
extending.explanation: The chain runs from first estimate to full answer: 20 × 4 gives about 80 riders per turn, 80 × 6 gives 480 an hour, and 3 hours carries 1,440 riders — while the place-value decomposition of 78.5 shows the precision you now attach to a number you once only estimated. The September questions did not change; the mathematician did.
extending.explanationEs: La cadena va de la primera estimación a la respuesta completa: 20 × 4 da unos 80 pasajeros por vuelta, 80 × 6 da 480 por hora y 3 horas llevan a 1,440 pasajeros, mientras que la descomposición por valor posicional de 78.5 muestra la precisión que ahora le pones a un número que antes solo estimabas. Las preguntas de septiembre no cambiaron; quien cambió fue el matemático.

practice.commonMistake: Treating your math story as finished — writing the same answers you wrote in Lesson 1-1 instead of looking for what actually changed. The story grows and evolves; a retrospective that copies September has missed the point.

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best captures this lesson's end-of-year summary of 'Math is Mine'?
choices: We are all doers of math in daily life, and our math stories continue to grow and evolve as we grow
Math belongs only to the students who mastered every unit this year
A math story is written once in September and never changes
Math stops mattering once the school year ends
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes both claims: everyone is a doer of math in daily life, and our stories keep growing and evolving as we advance.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has two parts: doers of math, and stories that keep growing.
Which option keeps both?
exitTicket.stemEs: ¿Qué afirmación capta mejor el resumen de fin de año de esta lección sobre «las matemáticas son mías»?
choicesEs: Todos hacemos matemáticas en la vida diaria, y nuestras historias matemáticas siguen creciendo y evolucionando conforme crecemos
Las matemáticas solo les pertenecen a los estudiantes que dominaron todas las unidades este año
Una historia de matemáticas se escribe una vez en septiembre y nunca cambia
Las matemáticas dejan de importar en cuanto termina el año escolar
exitTicket.explanationEs: El resumen hace las dos afirmaciones: todos hacemos matemáticas en la vida diaria, y nuestras historias siguen creciendo y evolucionando conforme avanzamos.
hintsEs: Vuelve a mirar la diapositiva de resumen.
Tiene dos partes: que todos hacemos matemáticas, y las historias que siguen creciendo.
¿Qué opción conserva las dos?

questions.stem: A bead pattern goes A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. What is the pattern unit?
choices: A, B, C
A
A, B, C, A, B, C
A, A, B, B, C, C
questions.explanation: The pattern unit is the shortest chunk that repeats — here, A, B, C.
questions.stemEs: Un patrón de cuentas va A, B, C, A, B, C, A, B, C. ¿Cuál es la unidad del patrón?
choicesEs: A, B, C, A, B, C
A, A, B, B, C, C
questions.explanationEs: La unidad del patrón es el trozo más corto que se repite — aquí, A, B, C.

questions.stem: A bead pattern repeats the unit A, B, C. What is the 10th bead?
choices: A
B
C
There is no 10th bead
questions.explanation: Three beads repeat, and 10 = 3 × 3 + 1. After 9 beads the unit restarts, so the 10th is A.
questions.stemEs: Un patrón de cuentas repite la unidad A, B, C. ¿Cuál es la 10.ª cuenta?
questions.explanationEs: Se repiten tres cuentas, y 10 = 3 × 3 + 1. Después de 9 cuentas la unidad vuelve a empezar, así que la 10.ª es A.

questions.stem: What makes a repeating design predictable?
choices: A pattern unit that repeats in the same order
Using many different colors
Making every piece a different size
Leaving gaps between the pieces
questions.explanation: Once you know the pattern unit and its order, you can predict any position in the design.
questions.stemEs: ¿Qué hace predecible un diseño que se repite?
choicesEs: Una unidad de patrón que se repite en el mismo orden
Hacer cada pieza de un tamaño distinto
questions.explanationEs: Una vez que conoces la unidad del patrón y su orden, puedes predecir cualquier posición del diseño.

questions.stem: A tile border repeats a 4-tile unit 6 times. How many tiles are in the border?
questions.explanation: The 4 tiles repeat 6 times, so multiply: 4 × 6 = 24. Adding gives 10.
questions.stemEs: Un borde de mosaicos repite una unidad de 4 mosaicos 6 veces. ¿Cuántos mosaicos hay en el borde?
questions.explanationEs: Los 4 mosaicos se repiten 6 veces, así que multiplica: 4 × 6 = 24. Sumar da 10.
